summary: Cuttyhunk Light on Cuttyhunk Island at the mouth of Buzzards Bay: lit in 1823, a skeletal tower from 1947, discontinued in 2005.

lens.note: fifth-order Fresnel lens from 1857 (LighthouseFriends); the USLHS record gives no year

structures.note: Taken down in 1860 when the square tower went up on the dwelling (LighthouseFriends).
Square tower and lantern room on the keeper's dwelling; the dwelling was demolished in 1891.
Temporary conical wooden tower linked to the frame dwelling by a covered way; demolished 1947.
Discontinued 2005 and removed. A stone oil house (1903) is the only remaining structure.

access.note: USLHS: not open to the public. LighthouseFriends: ferry to the island, a two-mile walk to the site, grounds open.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (per the USLHS and LighthouseFriends records)

events.note: Congress allocated $3,000 for a lighthouse on Cuttyhunk Island, or nearby
Conical stone tower and detached stone dwelling built
Light shown on 2 May 1823 with Benjamin Sayer as first keeper
Navy inspection by Lieutenant Edward W. Carpender found reflectors inadequately cleaned
I. W. P. Lewis complained the light was poorly placed and of little use
Lightship established on Sow and Pigs reef
Fifth-order Fresnel lens replaced lamps and reflectors
Second story added to keeper's dwelling; square tower and lantern room set on top; focal plane raised ten feet
31 January: keeper Samuel Austin Smith logged the schooner Connecticut striking the NW point; LighthouseFriends says Smith and John Black went out to save the crew
Old 1823 dwelling demolished; frame dwelling built on its foundation; temporary conical wooden tower built
11 March: British schooner Rob and Harry dismasted; drifted onto the west end of the island; steward Ephraim McKeil lost; keeper A. G. Eisener lit the wreck
24 February: British brig Aquatic struck the reef; Massachusetts Humane Society boat from Eisener's station capsized; five of six men lost
Stone oil house added to the station
Damaged in the Great Atlantic Hurricane
Wooden lighthouse and companion dwelling demolished; metal skeletal tower erected by the Coast Guard
Light on the skeletal tower discontinued
Skeletal tower removed; stone oil house remains

wrecks.vessel: Rob and Harry (British schooner, of St. John, New Brunswick)
wrecks.outcome: Dismasted in a gale; hulk drifted onto the west end of Cuttyhunk; steward Ephraim McKeil lost; lit by keeper A. G. Eisener about two hours later

wrecks.vessel: Aquatic (British brig, from Sagua to Boston with sugar)
wrecks.outcome: Stranded on the reef. Massachusetts Humane Society boat from the light's boathouse capsized; five of six men died, one (Josiah H. Tilton) was taken aboard the brig; the brig's crew were rescued the next day by the Cuttyhunk Life-Saving Station

corrections.why: The USLHS record says 'Demolished 1947, Replaced with a Steel Skeletal Tower'; LighthouseFriends says the skeletal tower was removed after 2005 and only a stone oil house remains.

corrections.proposed: conical stone tower, built 1823; wooden square tower added 1860
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends describes a stone tower in 1823 encased in brick twice, and the wooden square tower from 1860.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends and the USLHS record both say the light and its tower are gone; OpenStreetMap maps a structure at the site. The OSM point was not checked against an official source; the sources here say the site holds only a stone oil house.
The 1823 date is the first light (USLHS: 'Year Established: 1823'; LighthouseFriends: 2 May 1823). The 1947 date in Wikidata and Rowlett is the steel skeletal tower erected that year.

notes_for_editor: The Life-Saving Service station at Cuttyhunk is a separate station in this file (its keeper appears in the 1892 and 1893 narratives as the Life-Saving keeper, not the light). It is not in this story's chronology. Eisener is named in the 1892 and 1893 Life-Saving reports as light keeper and as keeper of the Massachusetts Humane Society's Lifeboat Station No. 43; the report names him as the keeper of the light, not the Life-Saving station. The 1892 narrative spells the vessel 'Bob and Harry' in its text (OCR); its heading reads 'ROB AND HARRY'; the index and the Life-Saving list read 'Rob and Harry'; the story uses 'Rob and Harry'. The Connecticut rescue (1872) rests on LighthouseFriends' quotation of the keeper's log and of an unnamed newspaper of the time; neither was read directly. The 1838 Carpender and 1842 Lewis inspections are quoted by LighthouseFriends; the originals were not read. Fanny Chase (1844-1847) and Ella F. Terpeny (1909) are head keepers in the USLHS roster and LighthouseFriends; neither record describes their service beyond the roster. Scan pages are used for the Life-Saving and Lighthouse Board volumes; printed pages in the 1893 Aquatic narrative (55-58) are read from the OCR page heads. The 1947 tower and 2005 discontinuance come from LighthouseFriends and the USLHS record; no Coast Guard source was read. Access: USLHS says not open to the public; LighthouseFriends says grounds open. Octave Ponsart's family memoir is cited only in LighthouseFriends and is not used. No NRHP check was made. Fact-check 2026-10-28: the story no longer calls Fanny Chase or Ella F. Terpeny women, since the roster and LighthouseFriends give no sex or gender and the names alone do not establish it. The 1892 Life-Saving narrative body prints 'Bob and Harry' and its heading 'ROB AND HARRY' (OCR); the index reads 'Rob and Harry'; the story uses Rob. The 1842 Lewis passage is cited to LighthouseFriends, which describes him as visiting the light, not as an inspector. The 1892 lighting sentence now quotes the report exactly ('fully two hours before the wreck was lighted by A. G. Eisener'), since the report does not say when she came to rest.
